clinicalPearls: Defined as carbohydrate intolerance first recognised during pregnancy, distinguishing it from pre-existing diabetes detected in early pregnancy
Diagnosis rests on an oral glucose tolerance test, usually performed around 24 to 28 weeks, or earlier in high-risk women
Risk factors include obesity, advanced maternal age, prior GDM, macrosomic infant, family history of diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and certain ethnic backgrounds
First-line management is medical nutrition therapy, glucose self-monitoring, and physical activity, with pharmacotherapy added if glycaemic targets are not met
Fetal complications include macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, birth trauma, neonatal hypoglycaemia, and polycythaemia
Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinaemia, which promotes excessive fetal growth and adiposity
Most women return to normal glucose tolerance after delivery, but there is a substantially increased lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes
Postpartum glucose testing is essential to detect persistent diabetes and to guide long-term risk reduction
reference.pathophysiology: Pregnancy is a progressively insulin-resistant state driven by placental hormones such as human placental lactogen, progesterone, and cortisol. Gestational diabetes develops when maternal pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion cannot compensate for this physiological resistance, leading to maternal hyperglycaemia. Glucose crosses the placenta freely and stimulates fetal insulin secretion; the resulting fetal hyperinsulinaemia acts as a growth factor causing macrosomia and, after cord clamping removes the maternal glucose supply, predisposes the neonate to hypoglycaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Pre-existing (overt) type 1 or type 2 diabetes unmasked in pregnancy
additionalInvestigations: Oral glucose tolerance test with fasting and post-load values
Home capillary glucose monitoring (fasting and postprandial) to guide therapy
HbA1c to help distinguish pre-existing diabetes when measured early
Serial fetal growth ultrasound and amniotic fluid assessment
Postpartum oral glucose tolerance test to reclassify glucose status
redFlags: Marked fetal macrosomia or polyhydramnios increasing risk of shoulder dystocia and stillbirth
Very poor glycaemic control suggesting undiagnosed overt diabetes
Reduced fetal movements or non-reassuring fetal surveillance
reference.prognosis: Well-controlled gestational diabetes has an excellent outcome, approaching that of the non-diabetic population. Poor control raises risks of macrosomia, operative delivery, birth trauma, and neonatal metabolic problems. Long term, affected women have a markedly increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, and their offspring have higher rates of obesity and glucose intolerance.
pitfalls: Missing overt pre-existing diabetes by not testing high-risk women in early pregnancy
Relying on symptoms, which are usually absent, rather than screening
Assuming a normal-sized fetus excludes risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia
Failing to arrange postpartum glucose reassessment and long-term follow-up
Neglecting neonatal glucose monitoring after delivery
management: Begin with medical nutrition therapy, capillary glucose self-monitoring, and physical activity as first-line management
Add pharmacotherapy when glycaemic targets are unmet, using insulin as the preferred agent and metformin as an alternative
Monitor the foetus with serial growth ultrasound and amniotic fluid assessment for macrosomia and polyhydramnios
Plan the timing and mode of delivery with attention to macrosomia and shoulder dystocia risk
Anticipate neonatal hypoglycaemia with early feeding and neonatal glucose monitoring
Coordinate care across obstetrics, the diabetes team, dietetics, and neonatology
Arrange postpartum oral glucose tolerance testing to reclassify glucose status and counsel on future type 2 diabetes risk
